newsitem.title: USA: Myriad of forces send US Treasuries sharply lower.
newsitem.headline: Myriad of forces send US Treasuries sharply lower.

text.p: A combination of fundamental and technical factors sent U.S. Treasury prices sharply lower on Thursday, pushing up yields to their highest levels in more than a week.
After posting only moderate losses for most of the session, a late-day selloff sent the 30-year bond down 31/32 to 99-20/32, while its yield rose to 6.65 percent from 6.58 percent on Wednesday.
Market participants said that profit-taking that began on Wednesday continued on Thursday.
"People were taking advantage of (low yields) to get out of (their positions)," said Chris Fitzmaurice, a bond trader at Salomon Brothers Inc.
A multitude of factors led to Thursday's selloff, traders noted, topped by unfriendly economic news, which gave the market a negative tone from the start that the market never recovered from.

Just after the market opened, the Labor Department reported a 1,000 rise in initial jobless claims in the week ended February 15 to 309,000. That was a low enough level to revive fears of a tight labor market.
In addition, Commerce reported a 2.0 percent rise in housing starts in January to a 1.350 million annual unit rate.

Treasuries dipped on the reports but recovered to pre-data levels, only to fall back once again after the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia said that its overall index of manufacturing activity jumped to 17.4 in February from 11.3 in January. New orders, shipments and prices also posted gains.
To make matters worse, the dollar fell substantially from Wednesday's levels against the yen and mark, leading to speculation foreign accounts would sell during Friday's overseas sessions.

"People are afraid the Japanese will be dumping paper," said one head trader at a U.S. primary dealership, noting that the selling would most likely be by retail accounts, which hold mostly longer-dated paper. That is in contrast to central banks, which buy mostly shorter dated Treasuries.

Bill Kirby, a trader at Prudential Securities Inc, said that once the selling started, it "snowballed." He noted that it stemmed from Wednesday's session, in which a bullish report of consumer prices failed to ignite a rally.
"There's no new money coming in to stem the tide," he said.

Treasuries did stabilize late morning and into the afternoon, with the two-year note down just 1/32 and the bond down 3/8-point. But just before the futures market closed, the March bond contract broke below a key level of 113-05, opening the floodgates for prices to fall further.
The bloodletting was halted when the contract held its 113-00 support level.
In the process, the yield curve steepened as short-term yields outperformed the intermediate and longer sectors.
Analysts said uncertainty surrounding near-term monetary policy should limit the upside in prices at the short end.
The bill sector was the lone bright spot for the Treasury market, as both the three- and six-month bill rates fell one basis point, to 4.95 percent and 5.02 percent, respectively.
The year-bill was up one basis point to 5.18 percent.

The two-year note closed down 2/32 at 100-2/32, yielding 5.84 percent. The five-year note fell 9/32 to 100-10/32 and yielding 6.18 percent. The 10-year note closed at 99, down 17/32. Its yield rose to 6.39 percent from 6.31 percent.
(( -- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1867 ))
